analysis.one_liner: Strips the National Labor Relations Board of its power to prosecute labor law violations and make binding rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; it died in the House Education and the Workforce Committee at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so the NLRB could investigate labor law violations but not prevent them, issue complaints, prosecute them before the Board, ask courts to enforce its orders, or seek injunctions [S2]. Workers alleging an employer broke labor law would instead have to bring their own lawsuit in federal court [S3]. The Board's rulemaking would be limited to its own internal procedures, blocking rules that affect the substantive rights of employers, employees, or unions [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers accused of firing or retaliating against workers for union activity. Today the NLRB's General Counsel investigates, prosecutes, and asks federal courts to enforce remedies, so an individual worker rarely has to sue alone; under this bill that machinery disappears and the burden falls on the worker [S2][S3]. Employers would also no longer face binding NLRB rules on matters like union elections or bargaining, since rulemaking would be confined to the Board's internal functions [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers accused of labor law violations

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the General Counsel's authority to issue and prosecute complaints of unfair labor practices before the Board, leaving the Board with investigation only [S2][S3].
Prohibits the Board from issuing any rule affecting the substantive rights of any person, employer, employee, or labor organization [S2][S3].
Allows a worker or union alleging a violation to bring a civil action in federal court, with the Board barred from seeking enforcement of its own orders or injunctions [S3].
Requires the Board to review and revise all existing regulations within six months of enactment to conform to the amendments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who face illegal retaliation for organizing. Instead of a government prosecutor pursuing their case at public expense, each worker would bear the cost and risk of a federal lawsuit, against an employer with far greater resources [S3]. Unions would lose the enforcement process they rely on when employers refuse to bargain or interfere with elections [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and unions filing labor complaints

drawbacks.text: It converts a publicly funded enforcement system into a do-it-yourself lawsuit: the text replaces Board prosecution with a private civil action in district court, meaning an individual worker pays court costs and lawyer fees to challenge an employer [S3].

It repeals the Board's authority to prevent unfair labor practices and to seek court enforcement or injunctions, so illegal firings or threats during a union drive could continue while an investigation and any private suit grind on [S2][S3].
It blocks any NLRB rule affecting substantive rights, ending the Board's ability to set modern procedures — for example, its election rules — through rulemaking [S2].

A good-faith argument for the change: supporters contend Board members are unelected officials who should not make substantive policy through rulemaking or act as both investigator and prosecutor; the bill addresses that by limiting the Board to investigation and internal functions [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to employers — less exposure to prosecution and fewer binding rules — comes directly at workers' expense. The existing system lets the government carry the cost of enforcing labor law; this bill moves that cost onto individual workers, who are the least able to bear it. There is no offsetting protection for workers in the text.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended with the bill dead [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Austin Scott introduced the bill on March 24, 2017 with 24 original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, its only committee action [S5].
It gathered 37 Republican cosponsors but never received a committee markup or a floor vote in the House, and it was never introduced in the Senate [S4][S5].
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill died without any vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions who depend on NLRB enforcement, since the enforcement system was left intact. Employers who wanted the Board's powers curtailed gained nothing because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who rely on NLRB enforcement

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors listed were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill went no further than a Republican-controlled committee referral [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers, especially those facing union organizing
industries.note: The bill removes the NLRB's power to prosecute unfair labor practices, seek injunctions, or issue substantive rules, sharply lowering the cost of firing or threatening workers during organizing drives [S2][S3]. The saving for employers is paid for by workers who lose their main protection.
Unions rely on NLRB complaint prosecution and court enforcement when employers interfere with organizing or bargaining; the bill repeals both, leaving unions to sue on their own [S2][S3].

The bill strips the Board and its General Counsel of complaint issuance, prosecution, rulemaking over substantive rights, and court enforcement — leaving investigation and internal functions only [S2][S3].
